entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Dome of the Rock (Qubbat al-Sakhra) is an Islamic shrine on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, built by Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan between 688 and 691 CE. The oldest surviving Islamic architectural monument, its golden dome has dominated Jerusalem's skyline for 1,330 years, making it the world's most recognizable religious building and the defining symbol of Islamic sacred architecture.

The Dome of the Rock was built over the Foundation Stone (the Sacred Rock), which Jewish tradition holds as the site where Abraham prepared to sacrifice Isaac, where Jacob dreamed of the ladder to heaven, and where the Holy of Holies of Solomon's Temple stood. Islamic tradition identifies it as the site from which Muhammad ascended to heaven during the Isra and Mi'raj. This triple sacred significance — to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — makes the Foundation Stone the most sacred square meter of earth in Abrahamic religion.

Abd al-Malik's construction was architectural and theological statement: the octagonal plan and Byzantine mosaic program challenged the Church of the Holy Sepulchre's circular plan; the dome's golden exterior (re-gilded with actual gold financed by Jordan's King Hussein in 1993) asserted Islamic splendor; and the Quranic inscriptions inside explicitly addressed Christian theology ('God has no son'). The Byzantine craftsmen who built it created a synthesis of Greco-Roman, Byzantine, and emerging Islamic aesthetics that defined Islamic architecture for centuries.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Dome of the Rock, built in 691 CE, is Islam's oldest surviving monument and its golden dome has been Jerusalem's defining image for 1,330 years — embodying the Abrahamic religions' most contested sacred geography.
